name: The Daily Battle Loop
recognitionLine: I don't want to be the phone police, but screens have become the fight we keep having.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Limits turn into arguments, bargaining, threats, taking the device, giving it back, and starting over. The screen issue has become a relationship issue.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: Screens may be serving a real emotional job, but the family only meets the loop at the point of conflict.
whatItMayBeCosting: Trust erodes. The parent gets exhausted. The child learns to defend the device instead of talking about what it's doing for them.
whatHelps: Move the conversation earlier than the limit moment. Build a predictable plan, reduce surprise enforcement, and name the pattern without making the child the problem.
whySupportMayHelp: Therapy can help the family stop repeating the same fight and work on the regulation, avoidance, or belonging need underneath the screen.

name: The Quiet Pull-Away
recognitionLine: They say they're fine, but I can feel them disappearing behind the screen.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Less family time, fewer offline interests, more closed doors, shorter answers, and a child who seems harder to reach.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: Screens may be offering privacy, comfort, identity, belonging, or a place to disappear when real life feels too exposed.
whatItMayBeCosting: The cost is not always a blow-up. Sometimes it's distance, loneliness, missed development, and a parent who starts grieving a kid who is still in the house.
whatHelps: Start with curiosity instead of interrogation. Look for one low-pressure bridge back into shared time, and don't make the first real conversation about taking the device away.
whySupportMayHelp: Support can help clarify whether this is normal privacy, stress, mood, social pain, or a deeper withdrawal pattern.

name: The Nighttime Off-Switch
recognitionLine: It doesn't feel like they're just staying up. It feels like the screen is how they get through the night.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Late-night use, devices in bed, hard mornings, irritability, school-day fatigue, and repeated promises that tonight will be different.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: The screen may be helping them avoid quiet, boredom, dread, loneliness, or the exposed feeling that shows up when the day finally stops.
whatItMayBeCosting: Sleep goes first. Then mood, patience, focus, family mornings, school capacity, and the parent's sense that every day starts behind.
whatHelps: Replace the off-switch before removing it. Build a wind-down that meets the actual night feeling: device parking, low-stimulation comfort, check-in time, and a plan for what happens when sleep feels hard.
whySupportMayHelp: Therapy can help a child build other ways to settle at night, especially when screens have become the only reliable off-switch.

name: The Social Mirror Loop
recognitionLine: Their mood rises and falls with a world I cannot see.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Checking posts, likes, group chats, streaks, views, comments, Snap Map, DMs, appearance content, or friend drama, followed by mood changes.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: Screens may be answering questions like: Am I included? Did I matter? Do I look okay? Where do I stand?
whatItMayBeCosting: Self-image, confidence, sleep, friendship stress, and family calm can all get pulled into invisible social signals.
whatHelps: Don't dismiss it as drama. Ask what the app makes them check for, reduce the highest-trigger features, and help them build self-worth measures that aren't only social metrics.
whySupportMayHelp: Therapy can help when social comparison, exclusion, or validation checking starts shaping mood, identity, or daily functioning.

name: The Always-Checking Loop
recognitionLine: They can't seem to settle unless they know what changed.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Quick checks throughout the day, repeated refreshing, anxiety when separated from the phone, and attention split between family life and whatever might update.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: The screen may be offering reassurance: nothing changed, no one is mad, no message was missed, no update has happened without them.
whatItMayBeCosting: Focus, sleep, patience, and presence get fragmented. The child may never get long enough away from the phone to learn the feeling can pass.
whatHelps: Stretch gaps gently, reduce unnecessary alerts, create predictable check windows, and work with the fear that checking is trying to quiet.
whySupportMayHelp: Therapy can help if checking has become the main way your child manages uncertainty, social worry, or the fear of missing something important.

name: The Online Belonging World
recognitionLine: Those people may really matter to them. The problem is that offline life is getting smaller.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Servers, group chats, fandoms, gaming groups, online communities, or creators become the main place the child feels known and expected.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: The online world may be giving real belonging, especially if offline life feels lonely, awkward, unsafe, or like nowhere fits.
whatItMayBeCosting: The risk is not that online belonging exists. The risk is that one online world starts holding too much: identity, mood, friendship, schedule, and self-worth.
whatHelps: Don't amputate the community. Understand what it gives them, then build one or two additional sources of belonging offline, nearby, or in healthier mixed spaces.
whySupportMayHelp: Therapy can help bridge online strengths back into offline life without shaming the community that may have been protecting them.

name: The Digital Competence Refuge
recognitionLine: In there, they know how to win. Out here, everything feels harder.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Games, rankings, streaks, stats, creator systems, edits, builds, or online projects become the place where effort feels clear and rewarding.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: The screen may be restoring competence and control when school, chores, relationships, sports, or life feel uncertain or defeating.
whatItMayBeCosting: The avoided offline area can decay, which makes the child feel even more behind and makes the refuge even more necessary.
whatHelps: Don't only remove the place they feel capable. Build small offline wins, shrink avoided tasks, and keep progress visible outside the screen too.
whySupportMayHelp: Therapy can help when screens are not just fun, but the only place a child feels effective, capable, or in control.

name: The Reward Chase Loop
recognitionLine: The next one could be the win, the drop, the pull, the trade, or the thing that makes it feel worth it.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Loot boxes, in-game purchases, sports betting, trading, marketplaces, gacha, rare drops, deals, secret spending, or repeated checking for wins.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: The screen may be offering hope and charge through uncertain rewards. The maybe-next-time feeling can become stronger than the actual prize.
whatItMayBeCosting: Money, secrecy, trust, sleep, school, and risk can escalate faster here than in most other loops.
whatHelps: Treat money and access seriously. Use parent-controlled limits, remove saved payment methods, document spending, and don't rely on willpower at the moment of reward.
whySupportMayHelp: Outside support is recommended when money, secrecy, loss chasing, or betting-like mechanics are part of the pattern.

name: The Intensity Loop
recognitionLine: They keep coming back more wired, more angry, or more impossible to reach.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: Drama, arguments, rage-bait, threat content, edgy videos, conflict, intense gaming, or online fights leave the child activated and irritable.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: The screen may be converting boredom, numbness, anxiety, or helplessness into intensity and certainty.
whatItMayBeCosting: The charge spills into the house. The child's baseline can become more reactive, and the family starts living around the next blow-up.
whatHelps: Separate the body charge from the content. Build decompression after intense use, reduce feeds that reward escalation, and create other ways to feel awake without conflict.
whySupportMayHelp: Therapy can help if intensity, anger, or conflict has become a main way your child regulates or feels in control.

name: The Autopilot Zone-Out
recognitionLine: It's not always a huge problem at once. It's the little disappearances all day.
whatYouMayBeSeeing: The child opens screens automatically in gaps, during chores, after school, while eating, during homework, in the bathroom, or whenever nothing is happening.
whatScreensMayBeDoing: The screen may be smoothing over boredom, transition friction, task-starting discomfort, or quiet moments before they can feel them.
whatItMayBeCosting: Time, attention, chores, homework, family presence, and small intentions leak away without one dramatic crisis.
whatHelps: Create choice points in the highest-friction gaps. Replace one automatic moment at a time instead of trying to overhaul the whole day.
whySupportMayHelp: Support can help when automatic use is connected to avoidance, attention problems, low mood, or family conflict around everyday routines.
